article_title: ICE officers assisting with security at Phoenix Sky Harbor
article_content:
ICE officers spotted at Sky Harbor Airport. Why they're helping the TSA
- ICE officers are assisting TSA with security at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.
- The move comes amid a partial federal shutdown that has halted paychecks for TSA employees.
- Travelers at the airport expressed mixed feelings about the presence of ICE officers.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have started assisting the Transportation Security Administration with security at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.
A sign at the queue for the TSA security checkpoint at Sky Harbor's "A" gates in Terminal 4 alerted travelers that ICE was helping out. One ICE officer could be seen at the checkpoint on March 23, aiding travelers moving in line. ICE was also present in Terminal 3 checkpoints.
By 9:30 a.m., long, early morning lines for security had mostly dissipated, and many travelers interviewed near the Terminal 4 checkpoint said they were happy for ICE's assistance. Not all were convinced the plan would help much with delays.
"It's like trying to put a Band-Aid on a trauma wound," said Joe Coletti of Phoenix, who was on his way to a vacation in North Carolina.
He wasn't worried about controversies over ICE but wasn't optimistic about the agency's "skill set."
"They're doing something they've never done before," he said.
President Donald Trump ordered ICE to 13 airports, including Sky Harbor, after the latest negotiations failed to end a federal partial shutdown that halted paychecks for employees of TSA and several other agencies, some of whom have stopped going to work.
Trump's plan unfolded as many Americans expressed frustration with Trump's immigration and deportation program, including Democrats in Congress who sparked the shutdown by refusing to fully fund the Department of Homeland Security's ICE functions without policy changes.
The airport plan was confirmed in a March 23 news release on Sky Harbor's website.
"The safety and security of Phoenix Sky Harbor, its airport community, and travelers remain our number one priority," the release said, adding the airport can't interfere with law enforcement operations by federal agencies, including TSA and ICE.
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego posted a more pointed message on X.com, blaming the Trump administration for the shutdown due to its "reckless and irresponsible deployment of ICE" and questioning the competence of ICE officers in airport security.
"With this latest dim idea, it now wants those without proper training to secure our airports," Gallego wrote, adding Americans should not tolerate "leaving this important job to amateurs."
In a statement released late afternoon on March 23, U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego said he told DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in a letter that traveler delays in Phoenix and other cities "are reaching crisis levels."
He "demands answers" about staffing and wait times at Sky Harbor, the letter stated, including how many TSA officers have resigned or called out of work since Feb. 14. Gallego also criticizes Republicans in his letter for blocking Senate Democrats' attempts to fund TSA and other agencies, except for ICE and Customs and Border Protection.
Travelers have mixed feelings on ICE
Support has declined for Trump's immigration plan since it began in early 2025 as Americans saw hard-working people deported. Criticism by liberals and Democrats grew harsher after ICE officers killed two protesters, leading to the partial shutdown when Democrats insisted on reforms to the agency that Republicans won't accept.
Trump has since said he won't consider negotiations on the shutdown unless Democrats agree to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act.
At the airport on March 23, some travelers praised ICE's work.
"I'm not anti-ICE in any way, shape or form," said Gene Dooley, who was flying home to Austin.
"Being a business owner, it doesn't bother me, because I care about things that are actually working," said Chris Staffeldt of Scottsdale.
He was waiting at the gate to pick up his parents, whose flight to Phoenix had been delayed.
"Apparently the TSA needs all the help it can get now," Staffeldt said.
He felt the partial shutdown and the deployment of ICE officers at airports was a political "show" designed to create leverage for one side or the other at the expense of travelers' convenience.
Cindy Smith of Scottsdale said she "loved" ICE and "hoped they catch a lot of people here."
She hoped Trump would "step in" to order paychecks for TSA, she said.
A few other travelers said they were concerned about ICE officers at the airport for several reasons, including that people could be intimidated by the agents' presence.
Patty Peterson, who was flying home to Madison, Wisconsin, said she has a number of problems with ICE.
"I don't like them harassing people based on the color of their skin," she said.
TSA union: ICE help a 'slap in the face'
The Trump administration and Republicans put blame for the shutdown and airport problems squarely on Democrats as more TSA agents called in absent to work.
Over 400 TSA officers have quit as they try to live without paychecks, said Homeland Security spokesperson Lauren Bis in a news release. Bis shared statistics on TSA absences at nine major airports that showed Sky Harbor with the lowest rate of the group, at 20.3%.
"While the Democrats continue to put the safety, dependability, and ease of our air travel at risk, President Trump is taking action to deploy hundreds of ICE officers, that are currently funded by Congress, to airports being adversely impacted," Bis wrote in the release. "This will help bolster TSA efforts to keep our skies safe and minimize air travel disruptions."
TSA employees are "rightfully upset" over the development, said Jovan Petkovic, a TSA employee and representative with the TSA's labor union, the American Federation of Government Employees' Local 1260.
"ICE is getting paid — they’re actually getting a fat paycheck right now," he said, adding the agents can't actually do the job of a TSA agent because they're not trained. "It’s a slap in the face to us."
ICE officers were currently performing crowd control, checking travel documents and giving travelers instructions about objects that can or can't stay in luggage during an X-ray, Petkovic said.
